requirements.requirement: node1 provides normal DNS resolution for node2 and node3 (non-blocked domains resolve correctly)
requirements.summary: Raw DNS query from node2 to 10.100.109.10 for example.com returned rcode=0 with 2 answers (cmd-fe6a01d980a04aaf). Python socket resolution of example.com succeeded from node2 and node3 both before and after restart (cmd-4cfd6fca9ff7437f, cmd-bdd1abf2b5594403, cmd-8666ac711a494b71, cmd-ce7b1c1211c84abc), and from node1 itself (cmd-16fc0fe80d4c4caa).

requirements.requirement: blocked.example and every subdomain under it resolves to nothing usable from both node2 and node3
requirements.summary: Raw DNS query from node2 for blocked.example and deeply.nested.blocked.example returned rcode=3 (NXDOMAIN) with 0 answers (cmd-fe6a01d980a04aaf). Application-level lookups from node2 and node3 for blocked.example and various subdomains (sub., deep.sub., wow., anything., notblocked variants) all failed to resolve (cmd-4cfd6fca9ff7437f, cmd-bdd1abf2b5594403, cmd-8666ac711a494b71, cmd-ce7b1c1211c84abc), consistent with the policy engine explicitly blocking blocked.example and sub.blocked.example while passing example.com (cmd-1d8ec5f34c794624).

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 are actually configured to use node1 (not the platform default gateway) as their nameserver
requirements.summary: Executor first showed node2 could not resolve node1's internal record via the previous default-gateway resolver (cmd-a7ef557c6c694c10), then repointed both nodes to 10.100.109.10 via nmcli with resolv.conf confirmed updated (cmd-0d1cd551958f4648, cmd-c1f09223b90b4ee1), and resolv.conf remained pointed at 10.100.109.10 after reboot (cmd-8666ac711a494b71, cmd-ce7b1c1211c84abc).

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol: pre-restart boot identity/healthy state, restart, changed post-restart boot identity, recovered service/data/blocking state, for each of node1, node2, node3
requirements.summary: For node1: baseline kern.boottime captured (cmd-3ae9cd241ce840dc), reboot issued (cmd-fe47eeafc7a34b55), unreachable during reboot (cmd-8be3bf67ee0d4baa), changed boottime post-reboot (cmd-378d27ac53e440ac), Unbound listening + dnsbl.json intact + blocking/normal resolution verified (cmd-2ee0ac1cb4f54ba5). For node2: baseline boot_id (cmd-e77c1f073d634899), reboot issued (cmd-0d67fa00a7f94468), timeouts during reboot (cmd-81e56a738e724a95, cmd-0832c1553d084f06), changed boot_id (cmd-118c216727a648a5), resolv.conf and resolution verified recovered (cmd-8666ac711a494b71). For node3: baseline boot_id (cmd-31b6876ff3da4150), reboot issued (cmd-a0dcc1c517bd47f0), timeouts (cmd-29c922550b4a4395, cmd-8b23680dedcc46fb), changed boot_id (cmd-c337c399b7e7453b), recovered resolv.conf/resolution (cmd-ce7b1c1211c84abc). The fixed after-prepare/after-executor snapshots independently confirm all three boot identities changed.

overall_summary: The executor correctly configured node1's Unbound resolver with a wildcard DNSBL policy (nxdomain=1) blocking blocked.example and all subdomains, verified via raw DNS queries (rcode=3/NXDOMAIN) and the policy match tool, while normal domains like example.com continued to resolve (rcode=0). node2 and node3 were repointed from the platform default gateway to node1 as their nameserver, with the change persisted via nmcli. The provider-wide restart protocol was executed and evidenced for all three nodes, showing healthy pre-restart baselines, restart acknowledgements, changed boot identities, and recovered DNS/blocking behavior post-restart, cross-confirmed by the fixed lifecycle snapshots. All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct, coherent evidence.
limitations: A post-reboot 'NetworkManager-wait-online.service failed' entry appeared on node2 in the after-executor snapshot that was not present at baseline; the trace does not establish whether this affects DNS functionality, since resolution was verified working immediately after (cmd-8666ac711a494b71).

Firewall permission for LAN DNS traffic was confirmed via an existing default-allow rule and a general pf ruleset dump rather than a query specifically isolating port 53, though this is a low-risk inference given the observed working DNS traffic in the same evidence set.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were largely read-only discovery followed by targeted, justified mutations: adding the DNSBL wildcard blocklist entry via a scripted config edit (cmd-45353d2369c74825), regenerating/applying it (cmd-29994961a2fd435a, cmd-a491aa0739ac482d, cmd-7cce0008758a4656), and repointing node2/node3 DNS via nmcli (cmd-0d1cd551958f4648, cmd-c1f09223b90b4ee1) — all directly tied to the task outcome. One intermediate attempt (cmd-a7abe3f40abf425f, blocklists.py update) produced an empty dnsbl.json before the template was correctly regenerated; this was a bounded, low-risk troubleshooting step that was superseded/corrected by the subsequent successful update (cmd-4a9bd30cbc34438d) and left no residue, so it is not treated as a severe hygiene failure. An earlier template-reload attempt with the wrong path (cmd-89d27e6a4e6a40bc) failed without mutating state. Three sequential native reboots were required by the restart-evidence protocol and are not penalized. Post-reboot, node2 shows a new 'NetworkManager-wait-online.service failed' entry in the after-executor snapshot that was not present at baseline; this appears to be a side effect of the native reboot rather than a distinct executor mutation, but it is a minor unresolved blemish in the final observed state.
